extracted.intended_audience: science journalists, editors, and communications officers who write or cover press releases about clinical trials
extracted.subtask_short: writing press releases for clinical trials
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing and evaluating press releases and associated news coverage of randomized controlled trials, with emphasis on accurate representation of trial conclusions and avoidance of misleading 'spin'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'spin' in reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Spin’ defined as specific reporting strategies (intentional or unintentional) emphasizing the beneficial effect of the experimental treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use language or framing that emphasizes benefit beyond what the trial data support. The page cites that 33 (47%) of press releases contained “spin”; 21 (51%) of associated news stories contained spin, often the same type. Anti-patterns include overstating efficacy, selective emphasis of positive outcomes, or omission of limitations that would temper conclusions. Authors/journalists should check whether claims exceed the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check the source of spin
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether any misleading emphasis originates in the scientific article’s abstract/conclusion, the press release, or the media coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study reported that spin frequently comes from the abstract (conclusions) of the published article rather than being introduced by the media. When preparing or covering a press release, verify the abstract’s wording and correct or contextualize any overstatements rather than merely repeating them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure conclusions appropriately reflect trial findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions reported should be an appropriate reflection of the trial findings and should not overinterpret or misinterpret the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers, editors, communications staff, and journalists should actively check that the wording of conclusions (in the abstract, press release, and news story) matches the strength and limits of the data. Avoid causal claims when only associations are shown or broad generalizations when evidence is limited. The authors explicitly recommend that reviewers and editors be particularly aware of this need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid giving readers unrealistic expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful that 'spin' could lead physicians and patients to overestimate the benefits of the treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether phrases or emphases in the release/story might create undue optimism. Include balanced statements about effect sizes, clinical relevance, uncertainty, and limitations to prevent misinterpretation by clinical audiences or the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose funding and the role of funders
rubrics_metrics.description: State funding sources and whether funders had any role in study design, data collection, analysis, decision to publish, or manuscript preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide transparent funding statements in the press release; the page gives an example: 'No direct funding was received for this study... No funding bodies had any role in the study design, data collection, analysis, decision to publish or preparation of the manuscript.' Failing to disclose funding or funder involvement is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose competing interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Declare authors’ competing interests or conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include explicit competing-interest statements (for example the page notes an author is a member of the journal’s editorial board and that no other competing interests exist). Press materials should mirror this transparency to help readers assess potential bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide access to the original article
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a link or reference to the freely available paper (or DOI) so readers and journalists can consult the full study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The press release instructs: 'IN YOUR COVERAGE PLEASE USE THIS URL TO PROVIDE ACCESS TO THE FREELY AVAILABLE PAPER' and supplies the DOI URL. Best practice: always supply an accessible link or DOI and indicate embargo status if applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include clear contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a named contact with email and phone for media enquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The example provides contact person, email, and phone (e.g., 'Contact: Sumrina Yousufzai syousufzai@plos.org 415-568-3164'). Good press releases include a media contact to enable clarification and reduce misreporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists should verify press release claims against the study
rubrics_metrics.description: News stories often repeat the same type of spin found in the press release and abstract; journalists must cross-check the original study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than reproducing the press release verbatim, reporters should read the abstract/full text to verify effect sizes, endpoints, statistical significance, and limitations. Anti-pattern: relying solely on press release language and thus amplifying any existing spin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors and reviewers share responsibility for downstream reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers and editors of published articles have an important role to play in the dissemination of research findings and should ensure conclusions are appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review and editorial processes should flag overstated conclusions in abstracts and insist on wording that accurately reflects findings. This upstream action reduces the likelihood that press releases and media coverage will propagate spin.
